name: Zoe Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the harp players for a large wedding orchestra, record practice passages and teach three advanced beginners. I have a master's degree in music and thirty-three years of paid playing. I like when a nervous couple hears the first harp notes and lets out a breath.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does that work mean for your household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, my partner runs a repair shop with steady earnings and our children are grown. We own our flat and have a year of expenses saved. I earn well for a senior musician, and plenty of orchestras play nearby, though none owes me a chair. I keep contracts in a paper folder and have never used AI.

say: I'd accept **faster printed notices** with rehearsal, travel and performance fees together.
I'd say a **harp player** still watches the couple enter.
think: Our **year of savings** and partner income cover a moved wedding.
The **orchestra and pupils** should continue through mild AI.
do: Confirm **nine paid ceremonies** and three pupils; request written cancellation terms.
Keep **paper contracts** and save one quarter of extra cleared fees after flat charges, food and strings.
feel: I feel **calm** while signed work and household income hold.
S0.quote: A wedding date can move without making us worry about supper.
fieldNote: Her **senior harp skill** earns high pay with a year's savings and many nearby orchestras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the orchestra that faster printed notices are fine if the rehearsal, travel and performance fees remain together. A harp still needs someone to watch the couple enter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A year's savings and my partner's shop income would cover a moved wedding. I expect the paid orchestra and pupils to continue if AI stays a small convenience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll confirm nine paid ceremonies and three pupils and request written cancellation terms for the next season. In the first year of mild AI I'll keep my paper contract folder and put a quarter of each extra cleared ceremony fee aside after flat charges, food and harp-string costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the season in the folder. A wedding date can move without making us worry about supper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened in the storm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A storm moved a reception last spring and the written term paid our travel plus half the performance. I still want the next contract signed before rehearsing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI scheduler?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't need an AI scheduler. I read the signed contract and ring the manager if a hall or fee looks wrong.

I'd keep **live fees** for playing and coaching separate from track pay.
think: Practice passages provide **one tenth** of my own pay.

do: Count **twelve passage invoices** and request a signed six-month playing calendar.
Offer **extra paid coaching** only after orders fall and manager books a written rate outside current calls.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a realistic recording-fee reduction.
S1.quote: A paid live lesson is useful only when the manager puts it on the sheet.
fieldNote: Her **small recording share** and large reserve let her insist on real paid coaching hours.

steps.text: Count twelve passage invoices and request signed six-month playing calendar

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the orchestra which paid practice-passage orders generated music might replace. I'd ask the manager to keep live playing and young-player coaching fees separate from recordings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Practice passages provide about one tenth of my pay. Losing them would matter, but our savings and local orchestras give me time to fill paid live dates if an opening exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll count the last twelve passage invoices and ask for a signed six-month playing calendar. In the first year, if passage orders fall, I'll offer extra paid rehearsal coaching only if the orchestra books it at a written rate outside current calls; I won't buy a new AI tool to chase a small recording fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real tenth of my own pay possibly shrinking. A paid live lesson is useful only when the manager puts it on the sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the manager booked extra coaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the manager has not booked extra coaching. I will count only signed hours, not a compliment about how I teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try a recording tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A colleague could show me a tool on her own nameless music under a paid-use licence and approved storage. I would still play each suggestion and stop if the note or file went wrong, but I am not paying for a trial.

Seek **posted paid harp tutor** after further live cuts; require master’s/teaching, paid in-person instruction, replacement net after travel/route.
Keep **orchestra and pupils** until a suitable signed offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected passage loss with search time.
S2.quote: A year's savings cannot tell me what pension income will arrive each month.
fieldNote: Expected **2028 one-tenth loss** precedes 2031 harp-playing robots; live cuts remain conditional.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the players that thinking AGI by 2028 could make practice passages before a robot plucks a harp. Harp-playing robots follow around 2031, so I would put live wedding calls in writing now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the passage orders to end in 2028, costing a tenth of my pay. I do not expect the signed live weddings to vanish at once, though I would search if they did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll total passage fees, request signed paid wedding calls and ask for actual pension statements before considering a stop at 60. In the first year after 2028, if live calls also fall, I'll seek a posted paid harp-tutor role only if my master's and teaching experience qualify, live in-person harp hand-position and practice coaching are paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the bus handles the hours; I'll keep the orchestra and pupils until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real tenth of pay disappearing, with a year saved and nearby employers giving me room to search. A collapse of live weddings would be a separate, worse condition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a tutor post open now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No music centre has offered me a tutor job. I would read a posted paid vacancy with real teaching hours before treating it as an option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not read a pension statement. A year's savings cannot tell me what pension income will arrive each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the orchestra that five years to AGI by 2031 is enough time to price paid apprentice coaching into the next live contract. Harp-playing robots follow around 2034, so someone must still show a young player a safe hand position before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordinary software may cheapen practice passages before 2031. I can mentor a younger harpist, but that hour must be paid by the orchestra and must not replace a booked performance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next season I'll ask the manager for a two-year written agreement naming a paid weekly apprentice-coaching hour, the orchestra's safe harp and insurance, my preparation pay and cancellation terms. In the first year after 2031, if passage fees end, I'll run that coaching only after the manager signs the paid hour, the instrument is checked, the apprentice attends and the slot stays outside booked playing and pupil time; without those terms I'll keep existing paid shows and lessons instead of counting a mentoring wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the passage fees, though paid teaching I already know could replace some of them. A gifted apprentice is not a fee until someone books my hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who provides a safe harp?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The orchestra owns the teaching harp and would have its technician check strings and frame. I won't lend my concert harp to cover a missing insured instrument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the coaching agreement been signed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the agreement has not been signed. I will not make a young player's promise pay for a date the manager has not booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown children that ten years to AGI by 2036 lets us read pension figures and paid wedding contracts before choosing a stopping date. Harp-playing robots follow around 2039, but the flat still needs its monthly charges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still want to play and coach. A year of savings and our flat help, but I have not seen what any pension will actually pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request actual pension statements and a written two-year paid ceremony plan, then save a quarter of each extra cleared wedding fee after flat charges, food and harp strings toward fifteen months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep paid orchestra and pupil work while booked and take apprentice coaching only with signed orchestra pay for my hour/preparation, a checked insured harp and no clash; if live work falls and pension figures leave a gap, I'll seek a posted paid harp-tutor role only if my master's and teaching qualify, live in-person harp hand-position and practice coaching are paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the bus works, keeping current work until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about pay that far ahead while present work and a year's reserve are sound. I would slow only after a pension confirmed payable for that period and signed fees cover our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra wedding pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no extra wedding pays, there is no quarter to save from that source. I won't take money needed for flat charges to meet a target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen your pension figure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have not seen the pension figure. I will read it with my partner before declining a paid show.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because practice-passage fees could disappear before I know whether wedding calls hold. Signed ceremonies, actual pension figures and a posted qualified harp-tutor role with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the lead player to ready a young harpist before a show. A beautiful lesson is still unpaid work without a signed hour.

headlineQuote: A beautiful lesson is still unpaid work without a signed hour.
portrait: Zoe is a **58-year-old senior harp leader** with a music master's degree, partner and grown children.
Her **higher pay**, year of savings and many nearby orchestras allow time to search if a small track share ends.
She **never uses AI** and relies on signed paper contracts.
She offers **paid apprentice coaching** only through a signed orchestra hour with safe insured harp and protected current work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove Zoe's one-tenth practice-passage income before live calls are certain.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed wedding calls**, actual pension figures and posted qualifying human harp teaching with written after-travel pay would help.
